body:
Childhood & Early Life

Mary Sidney was born around 1587 at Penshurst Place in Kent, into one of the most literary families in England. Her uncle was Sir Philip Sidney, the soldier-poet who died young and became a legend, and her aunt was Mary Sidney Herbert, Countess of Pembroke, who translated the Psalms and ran a kind of writers' salon. Mary grew up with a library, an example, and the unspoken expectation that she'd be clever. Her father, Robert Sidney, was often away on service, and her mother Barbara kept the household together.

What She Did & Why She's Remembered

Lady Mary Wroth wrote the first known work of prose fiction by an Englishwoman, The Countess of Montgomery's Urania (1621), a huge romance, and she attached to it a sonnet sequence, Pamphilia to Amphilanthus. She wrote as a woman speaking about her own desire, not as the object of a man's poem. In a Petrarchan tradition where the woman is silent and cruel, Wroth makes the woman the lover, and the one who is left waiting.

Family Life

At about seventeen she was married to Sir Robert Wroth, a rich landowner and hunter who was much older. By most accounts it was not a happy match, and he spent a lot of her fortune. In March 1614 he died, leaving heavy debts, and their baby son, James, died soon after. She was a widow in her twenties with nothing but debt and a name.

Romantic Life

After her husband's death she began a long love affair with her cousin William Herbert, third Earl of Pembroke, a charming, famously unfaithful courtier. She had two children by him, Katherine and William, and he never married her. Her sonnets read like a diary of that situation, a woman loyal to a man who wasn't, writing her way through absence, jealousy and wanting. If you recognise the pattern, so did she; the poems are her taking it apart in public.

Life Until Death

When the Urania came out in 1621, the court spotted real people in it. Lord Edward Denny took it as a slander on his family and attacked her in vicious verse, calling her a "hermaphrodite in show" and telling her to leave writing alone. Wroth fired back with a furious answer of her own and then withdrew the book from sale. She stayed in debt for years and drifted out of public view. She died around 1651, and a second part of the Urania stayed in manuscript until modern times.

Their Works

These are four pieces from Pamphilia to Amphilanthus, with her original seventeenth-century spelling kept as printed.

Pamphilia to Amphilanthus 17
Sweet shades why doe you seeke to give delight
To mee who deeme delight in this vilde place
Butt torment, sorrow, and mine owne disgrace
To taste of joy, or your vaine pleasing sight;
Show them your pleasures who saw never night
Of greife, wher joyings fauning, smiling face
Appeers as day, wher griefe found never space
Yett for a sigh, a grone, or envies spite;
Butt O on mee a world of woes doe ly,
Or els on mee all harmes strive to rely,
And to attend like servants bound to mee,
Heat in desire, while frosts of care I prove,
Wanting my love, yett surfett doe with love
Burne, and yett freeze, better in hell to bee.
Pamphilia to Amphilanthus 7
Love leave to urge, thou know’st thou hast the hand;
’T’is cowardise, to strive wher none resist:
Pray thee leave off, I yeeld unto thy band;
Doe nott thus, still, in thine owne powre persist,
Beehold I yeeld: lett forces bee dismist;
I ame thy subject, conquer’d, bound to stand,
Never thy foe, butt did thy claime assist
Seeking thy due of those who did withstand;
Butt now, itt seemes, thou would’st I should thee love;
I doe confess, t’was thy will made mee chuse;
And thy faire showes made mee a lover prove
When I my freedome did, for paine refuse.
Yett this Sir God, your boyship I dispise;
Your charmes I obay, butt love nott want of eyes.
Pamphilia to Amphilanthus 19
Come darkest night, becoming sorrow best;
Light; leave thy light; fitt for a lightsome soule;
Darknes doth truly sure with mee oprest
Whom absence power doth from mirthe controle:
The very trees with hanging heads condole
Sweet sommers parting, and of leaves distrest
In dying coulers make a griefe-full role;
Soe much (alas) to sorrow are they prest,
Thus of dead leaves her farewell carpett’s made:
Theyr fall, theyr branches, all theyr mournings prove;
With leavles, naked bodies, whose huese vade
From hopefull greene, to wither in theyr love,
If trees, and leaves for absence, mourners bee
Noe mervaile that I grieve, who like want see.
Song from Pamphilia to Amphilanthus
Time only cause of my unrest
By whom I hop’d once to bee blest
How cruell art thou turned?
That first gav’st lyfe unto my love,
And still a pleasure nott to move
Or change though ever burned;
Have I thee slack’d, or left undun
One loving rite, and soe have wunn
Thy rage or bitter changing?
That now noe minutes I shall see,
Wherein I may least happy bee
Thy favors soe estranging.
Blame thy self, and nott my folly,
Time gave time butt to bee holly;
True love such ends best loveth
Unworhty love doth seeke for ends
A worthy love butt worth pretends
Nor other thoughts itt proveth:
Then stay thy swiftnes cruell time,
And lett mee once more blessed clime
To joy, that I may prayse thee:
Lett mee pleasure sweetly tasting
Joy in love, and faith nott wasting
And on fames wings I’le rayse thee:
Never shall thy glory dying
Bee untill thine owne untying
That time noe longer liveth;
T’is a gaine such tyme to lend:
Since soe thy fame shall never end
Butt joy for what she giveth.
epi: The first Englishwoman to write a romance, and a sonnet sequence from the woman's side of the heartbreak
